# Session preparation

## Installing R packages

You will need to install the following packages from CRAN:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("patchwork", "dplyr", "tidyr", "suncalc", "remotes",
  "tidyverse", "classInt", "data.table", "ctmm", "sp", "sf", "leaflet", "htmlwidgets))

```
<br>
And from GitHub:

- **FathomR**
```{r, eval = FALSE}

remotes::install_github("Fish-Tracking-Data-Team/FathomR",
  build_vignettes = TRUE,
  dependencies = TRUE)

```

- **RangeR**
```{r, eval = FALSE}

remotes::install_github("Fish-Tracking-Data-Team/RangeR",
                        build_vignettes = TRUE,
                        dependencies = TRUE)
```

- **gapFinder**
```{r, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("IMOS-AnimalTracking/gapFinder",
  build_opts = c("--no-resave-data", "--no-manual"),
  build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

- **remora**

```{r, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("IMOS-AnimalTracking/remora",
  build_vignettes = TRUE,
  dependencies = TRUE)
```

For interactive use, set your working directory to the folder containing the workshop materials. When rendering, R Markdown uses the directory containing this document:

```{r}
options(width = 70) # Console width setting
```

## 1.4. Receiver performance and diagnostics - gapFinder package walkthrough

### Load packages

```{r gapfinder-packages}
library(FathomR)
library(gapFinder)
library(patchwork)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(suncalc)
```

### Load receiver logs

Load Fathom csv files exported from [Fathom Central](https://fathomcentral.com/learn) and stored on disk:

```{r gapfinder-load}
fathom_dets <- parse_fathom_files("Data/gapFinder/Fathom",
  output = "list")
```

### Match deployment metadata

The raw receiver log files will need to be matched to receiver deployment metadata, so that gapFinder can assing them to the correct stations, and process only the data for when the receivers were in the water. 

```{r gapfinder-metadata}
# Example metadata file
meta_file <- read.csv("Data/gapFinder/Receiver metadata.csv")

meta_file

```
```{r, results = "hide"}
# Match metadata and Fathom files
dets_sort <- match_meta(input = fathom_dets,
  path_meta = "Data/gapFinder/Receiver metadata.csv",
  receiver_id = "receiver_name",
  transmitter_id = "transmit_id",
  type = "type",
  station_name = "station_name",
  deploy_datetime = "receiver_deployment_datetime",
  recover_datetime = "receiver_recovery_datetime",
  lat = "receiver_deployment_latitude",
  lon = "receiver_deployment_longitude",
  tz = "UTC")
```
```{r, gapFinder-match_meta}
names(dets_sort)

# Detections
head(as.data.frame(dets_sort$det))

# Diagnostic
head(as.data.frame(dets_sort$diag))
```

### Daily transmissions and detections

The first step in data analyses is to indentify how many range test transmissions could be successfuly detected (detection efficiency). This step can be done at both **daily** resolution, or separately for day/night periods (using ```circadian = TRUE```). There is no need to set timezones, gapFinder will automatically use your receiver deployment locations to figure it out.

```{r gapfinder-daily-dets}
# Calculate daily detections
daily_dets <- get_daily_dets(input = dets_sort,
  circadian = TRUE,
  path_meta = "Data/gapFinder/Receiver metadata.csv",
  receiver_id = "receiver_name",
  transmitter_id = "transmit_id",
  station_name = "station_name",
  type = "type",
  deploy_datetime = "receiver_deployment_datetime",
  recover_datetime = "receiver_recovery_datetime",
  lat = "receiver_deployment_latitude",
  lon = "receiver_deployment_longitude",
  tz = "UTC")

head(daily_dets)
```

#### Calculating daily detection ranges

The next step will be to calculate the daily ranges for each station in the array. If you run ```get_daily_dets``` with ```circadian = TRUE```, the ranges will be automatically calculated separately for day/night periods. Otherwise, ranges will be calculated with daily resolution.

The machine learning correction model will also be applied to all calculated ranges, if receiver diagnostic data is available (receiver was recovered). 

```{r gapfinder-daily-ranges}
daily_ranges <- get_daily_ranges(input = daily_dets,
  diag_data = dets_sort,
  parallel = TRUE)

names(daily_ranges)
daily_ranges$global # Global parameters
head(daily_ranges$ranges)
head(daily_ranges$curves)
```

We can use the $ranges and $curves objects to reconstruct the daily range curves for each day (and circadian period) of data available.

```{r gapfinder-curves, fig.height = 12}
dates <- seq(as.Date("2022-12-29", tz = "UTC"),
  as.Date("2023-01-02", tz = "UTC"),
  1)

dates

for (i in 1:length(dates)) {
  aux_plot <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
    geom_line(data = subset(daily_ranges$curves,
        station_name == "MIL 10" &
        date == dates[i]),
      aes(x = x, y = p),
      linewidth = 1,
      colour = "dodgerblue") +
    geom_point(data = subset(daily_ranges$ranges,
        station_name == "MIL 10" &
        date == dates[i]),
      aes(x = max_distance_detected, y = daily_efficiency),
      size = 3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, lty = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "Distance (m)", y = "Detection prob (%)",
      title = paste("Date:", dates[i])) +
    facet_wrap(~circadian)

  # Combine plots
  if (i == 1) {
    plot_curve <- aux_plot
  } else {
    plot_curve <- plot_curve / aux_plot
  }
}

plot_curve
```

gapFinder also has a **range diagnostics** function, that returns several summary statistics of range for each station (and circadian period).

```{r gapfinder-diagnostics}
diag_ranges <- range_diag(input = daily_ranges,
  station_order = c("MIL 10"))

as.data.frame(diag_ranges)
```

We can use $ranges to plot the range timeseries (range = modelled range; cor_range = machine learning corrected ranges) for each station.

```{r gapfinder-ranges-plot}
ranges_long <- daily_ranges$ranges %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(cor_range, range),
    names_to = "range_type",
    values_to = "range_value"
  )

plot_ranges1 <- ggplot(ranges_long) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(aes(x = date, y = range_value, colour = range_type)) +
  facet_wrap(~circadian, nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Range (m)", colour = "",
    title = "MIL 10 daily ranges")

plot_ranges2 <- ggplot(ranges_long) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = circadian,
    y = range_value,
    group = interaction(circadian, range_type),
    colour = range_type)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Range (m)", colour = "")

plot_ranges <- (plot_ranges1 | plot_ranges2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

plot_ranges
```

#### Environmental drivers of detection range

First we need to add circadian periods to the diagnostic data (OBS: to be added as a function in the package in the next update).

gapFinder defines day/night periods using **nautical dawn** and **nautical dusk** as the periods of reference. 

First, lets use a single location reference point:

```{r gapfinder-circadian}

lat <- dets_sort$diag$receiver_deployment_latitude[1]

lat 

lon <- dets_sort$diag$receiver_deployment_longitude[1]

lon 

# Parse timestamps in UTC, then derive the local time and local date
dets_sort$diag <- dets_sort$diag %>%
  mutate(
    local_time = with_tz(Time, "Australia/Hobart"),
    date = as.Date(local_time) # local calendar date, used for the join
  )

# Sunrise and sunset for each local date at receiver deployment
sun <- getSunlightTimes(
  date = unique(dets_sort$diag$date),
  lat = lat,
  lon = lon,
  keep = c("nauticalDawn", "nauticalDusk"),
  tz = "Australia/Hobart"
)

head(sun)

# Assign day/night categories
dets_sort$diag <- dets_sort$diag %>%
  left_join(
    sun %>% dplyr::select(date, nauticalDawn, nauticalDusk),
    by = "date"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    circadian = case_when(
      local_time >= nauticalDawn & local_time < nauticalDusk ~ "day",
      TRUE ~ "night"
    )
  )

# Sanity check
table(dets_sort$diag$circadian, useNA = "ifany")
```

Plot diagnostic data and daily ranges:

```{r gapfinder-diag-plots, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 10}
plot_eff <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
  geom_line(data = daily_ranges$ranges,
    aes(x = date, y = daily_efficiency)) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Efficiency (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~circadian, nrow = 2)

plot_temp <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
  geom_line(data = dets_sort$diag,
    aes(x = Time, y = as.numeric(`Ambient Temperature (deg C)`))) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Temperature (°C)") +
  facet_wrap(~circadian, nrow = 2)

plot_noise <- ggplot() + theme_bw() +
  geom_line(data = dets_sort$diag,
    aes(x = Time, y = as.numeric(`Noise Mean (mV)`))) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Noise (mV)") +
  facet_wrap(~circadian, nrow = 2)

plot_diag <- plot_eff | plot_temp | plot_noise
```

```{r gapfinder-combined, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 12}
plot_ranges / plot_diag
```

## 2.2. Home range analysis and habitat associations

### 2.2.1 Load packages and sample positions 
```{r, home_range_packages}

# - continuous time movement modeling (CTMM) from fine-scale positioning data 
# - The workflow below covers the quantitative assessment of range residency 
#   and area utilisation while taking into account autocorrelation structures in tracking data. 
# - If estimates of positional error are available, CTMM can incorporate uncertainty when calculating space use. 
# - CTMM can handle irregular sampling intervals.


# 1. Load packages and example data 
library(ctmm)
library(sf)
library(sp)

# Example positional data from two fish
fish_61043 <- read.csv("Data/home_range/BT61043_great_lake_position_data.csv")
fish_61065 <- read.csv("Data/home_range/BT61065_great_lake_position_data.csv")


```

### 2.2.2 Examine animals positions 

```{r, home_range_tracks}
# When enabled, ctmm imports HPE as HDOP (relative horizontal error).
# HPE is a unitless measure of sensitivity to positioning error

use_hpe <- FALSE

tracks <- list(fish_61043 = fish_61043, fish_61065 = fish_61065)
for (id in names(tracks)) {
  fixes <- tracks[[id]][, c("Time", "Longitude", "Latitude")]
  if (use_hpe) {
    fixes$HPE <- tracks[[id]]$HPE
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(fixes$HPE)), all(fixes$HPE > 0))
  }
  fixes <- fixes[complete.cases(fixes), ]
  fixes <- unique(fixes[order(fixes$Time), ])
  fixes$individual.local.identifier <- id
  tracks[[id]] <- as.telemetry(fixes, timeformat = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS",
                              timezone = "UTC")
}

# Put both fish in the same coordinate system BEFORE fitting their models.
projection(tracks) <- projection(tracks[[1]])

# 2. Inspect the tracks ----------------------------------------------------

plot(tracks, col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), error = FALSE,
     main = "Great Lake fish tracks", cex = 1.5)
legend("topright", legend = names(tracks),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), pch = 16, bty = "n")

```

### 2.2.3 Construct Variograms and model fitting
```{r, home_range_variograms}
# 3. Explore autocorrelation and select movement models --------------------
# A variogram shows how displacement changes with time lag. A plateau can
# support a bounded home range; inspect the curve before interpreting AKDE.
# IID: independent positions; OU: correlated positions;
# OUF: correlated positions and velocities. Anisotropic = direction-dependent.

# With use_hpe = TRUE, include error whose size is proportional to HPE.
# With no stationary-tag calibration supplied, estimate the scale together
# with movement. error = 1 is a starting guess, NOT a fixed 1-metre error.

# FALSE: faster computation without location-error fitting.
# TRUE: include HPE in home range estimation (much slower).

# Calibration data are preferable: simultaneous fitting can confound movement
# and location error. See vignette("error") for the calibrated approach.
# With use_hpe = FALSE, the model does not account for location error.
variograms <- list()
candidate_models <- list()
models <- list()

# check the number of CPU cores available for calculation

parallel::detectCores()

##### THE FOLLOWING SECTION IS SLOW

# per fish. trace = TRUE prints progress as candidate models are fitted.

#   plot(variograms[[id]], main = paste(id, "empirical variogram"))

#                       CTMM = ctmm(error = if (use_hpe) 1 else FALSE),
#                       variogram = variograms[[id]],
#                       interactive = FALSE)
#   candidate_models[[id]] <- ctmm.select(tracks[[id]], guess,
#                                         verbose = TRUE, trace = TRUE, cores = 14) #ctmm.select will select the optimal model basesd on AIC
  
#   models[[id]] <- candidate_models[[id]][[1]]
#   print(summary(candidate_models[[id]]))
#   print(summary(models[[id]]))

#   plot(variograms[[id]], CTMM = models[[id]], main = paste(id, "model fit"))
#   # Lag limits are in seconds, even if the displayed axis uses hours.
#   plot(variograms[[id]], CTMM = models[[id]], xlim = c(0, 6 * 60 * 60), # short temporal variogram 
#        main = paste(id, "first 6 hours"))
# }
```

```{r home_range_variogram plots}

### TO SAVE TIME, WE ARE LOADING OUTPUTS FROM A PREVIOUS RUN
# to save time, let's load previous model run
great_lake <- readRDS('outputs/ctmm_example/great_lake_analysis.rds')

variograms <- great_lake$variograms
models <- great_lake$models

for (id in names(great_lake$tracks)) {
  plot(variograms[[id]], CTMM = models[[id]], main = paste(id, "model fit"))
  # Lag limits are in seconds, even if the displayed axis uses hours.
  plot(variograms[[id]], CTMM = models[[id]], xlim = c(0, 6 * 60 * 60), # short temporal variogram 
       main = paste(id, "first 6 hours"))

}
```



### 2.2.4 Calculate AKDE space use areas 

```{r, home_range_AKDE}
# 4. Estimate home ranges within the lake ----------------------------------

# AKDE utilisations can be constrained using hard boundaries such a river banks, coastlines or lake shorelines 
# load the hard boundary of the lake shoreline, projection is WGS84

lake <- st_read("Data/home_range/great_lake_hard_boundary_wgs84.shp",
                quiet = TRUE)
lake <- st_transform(lake, st_crs(ctmm::as.sf(tracks[[1]])))
lake_boundary <- as(lake, "Spatial")

# AKDE = autocorrelated kernel density estimation.
# A UD (utilization distribution) describes estimated long-term space use.
# SP.in = TRUE restricts space use to the hard boundary polygon.
# Fit both UDs together so they share the grid needed for overlap analysis.

home_ranges <- akde(tracks, models, SP = lake_boundary, SP.in = TRUE)

# calculate the space use area for the 50% and 95% home range contours.
# level = 0.95 gives 95% confidence limits on range contours.
# CI contours describe area uncertainty, not uncertainty in boundary location.

area_summaries <- list()
for (id in names(tracks)) {
  area_summaries[[id]] <- data.frame()
  for (range_level in c(0.50, 0.95)) {
    # units = FALSE returns square metres; divide by 1e6 to report km^2.
    area_ci <- summary(home_ranges[[id]], level.UD = range_level,
                       level = 0.95, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6
    area_summaries[[id]] <- rbind(area_summaries[[id]], data.frame(
      home_range_percent = 100 * range_level,
      low_km2 = area_ci[1, "low"], estimate_km2 = area_ci[1, "est"],
      high_km2 = area_ci[1, "high"]))
    plot(tracks[[id]], UD = home_ranges[[id]],
      level.UD = range_level, level = 0.95,
     main = paste(id, 100 * range_level, "% home range with 95% CIs"))
    points(tracks[[id]])
  }
  print(id)
  print(area_summaries[[id]])
}
``` 

### 2.2.5 Calculate areas of overlap and proximity
```{r, home_range_overlaps}
# 5. Compare space use and potential encounter locations -------------------
home_range_overlap <- overlap(home_ranges)
home_range_overlap$CI                  # Estimates and confidence intervals.
home_range_overlap$CI[, , "est"]      # Matrix of overlap estimates.
# Bhattacharyya overlap: 0 = no shared space, 1 = identical distributions.
# Shared space alone does not show that fish met at the same time.

encounter_locations <- cde(home_ranges)
plot(encounter_locations, DF = "PDF", col.UD = "purple",
     col.level = "purple", col.grid = NA,
     main = "Potential encounter locations")
# CDE = conditional distribution of encounters: where encounters would be
# expected from long-term space use, conditional on an encounter occurring.
# This map does not identify observed meetings.


# Distances require the tracks AND fitted models, rather than home-range UDs.
# Predictions align the fish at shared times within their overlapping records.
fish_distances <- distances(tracks, models)
head(fish_distances)
plot(fish_distances$timestamp, fish_distances$est, type = 'l')

``` 

### 2.2.6 Export data for reuse
```{r, home_range_exports}
# 6. Save the analysis so you can return to it without refitting ------------
output_dir <- "outputs/ctmm_example"
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(use_hpe = use_hpe, tracks = tracks, variograms = variograms,
             candidate_models = candidate_models, models = models,
             home_ranges = home_ranges, area_summaries = area_summaries,
             overlap = home_range_overlap,
             encounter_locations = encounter_locations,
             distances = fish_distances),
        file.path(output_dir, "great_lake_analysis.rds"))

# Each table contains the 50% and 95% ranges and their 95% area CIs in km^2.
for (id in names(tracks)) {
  write.csv(area_summaries[[id]], file.path(output_dir, paste0(id, "_area.csv")),
            row.names = FALSE)
}

```

### 2.2.7 Mapping the results
```{r leaflet map}
# Visualise results wuith the interactive map of tracks and home ranges ---------------------
# Run once if needed: install.packages(c("leaflet", "htmlwidgets"))


library(leaflet)
library(htmlwidgets)

# To map a saved analysis in a fresh R session, first load ctmm and sf, then:
# results <- readRDS("outputs/ctmm_student/great_lake_analysis.rds")
# tracks <- results$tracks
# home_ranges <- results$home_ranges
# encounter_locations <- results$encounter_locations

# create some unique colours for each fish
fish_colors <- c(fish_61043 = "steelblue", fish_61065 = "tomato")

# combine track points into single object
all_track_points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tracks, function(track) {
  st_transform(ctmm::as.sf(track), 4326)
}))

# set boundaing box
map_bounds <- st_bbox(all_track_points)

# invoke leaflet maps
fish_map <- leaflet(options = leafletOptions(preferCanvas = TRUE)) %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  fitBounds(lng1 = map_bounds[["xmin"]], lat1 = map_bounds[["ymin"]],
            lng2 = map_bounds[["xmax"]], lat2 = map_bounds[["ymax"]])
map_groups <- character()

for (id in names(tracks)) {
  # Leaflet needs longitude/latitude coordinates (EPSG:4326).
  track_points <- st_transform(ctmm::as.sf(tracks[[id]]), 4326)
  for (range_level in c(0.95, 0.50)) {
    range_polygons <- st_transform(ctmm::as.sf(home_ranges[[id]],
      level.UD = range_level, level = 0.95), 4326)
    # Keep the estimate and both confidence-limit contours from ctmm.
    is_estimate <- grepl(" est$", range_polygons$name)
    ci_polygons <- range_polygons[!is_estimate, ]
    ci_labels <- ifelse(grepl(" low$", ci_polygons$name), "Lower", "Upper")
    range_group <- paste(id, paste0(100 * range_level, "% home range"))
    ci_group <- paste(range_group, "95% CI")
    map_groups <- c(map_groups, range_group, ci_group)

    fish_map <- fish_map %>%
      addPolygons(data = range_polygons[is_estimate, ], color = fish_colors[[id]],
                  weight = 2, fillOpacity = 0.15,
                  group = range_group, popup = paste(range_group, "estimate")) %>%
      addPolygons(data = ci_polygons, color = fish_colors[[id]],
                  weight = 1.5, fill = FALSE, dashArray = "5, 5",
                  group = ci_group,
                  popup = paste(range_group, paste(ci_labels, "95% area CI limit"),
                                sep = "<br>"))
  }

  map_groups <- c(map_groups, paste(id, "track"))
  fish_map <- fish_map %>%
    addCircleMarkers(data = track_points, color = fish_colors[[id]],
                     radius = 2, stroke = FALSE, fillOpacity = 0.7,
                     group = paste(id, "track"),
                     popup = paste(id, format(track_points$timestamp,
                                   tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE), sep = "<br>"))
}

# CDE combines both fish, so add its estimated 50% encounter hotspot once.
# Transform it to longitude/latitude before handing it to Leaflet.
encounter_polygons <- st_transform(
  ctmm::as.sf(encounter_locations, level.UD = 0.50, level = 0.95),
  4326
)
encounter_group <- "50% potential encounter hotspot"
encounter_estimate <- encounter_polygons[grepl(" est$", encounter_polygons$name), ]
map_groups <- c(map_groups, encounter_group)
fish_map <- fish_map %>%
  addPolygons(data = encounter_estimate, color = "purple", weight = 2,
              fillColor = "purple", fillOpacity = 0.20, group = encounter_group,
              popup = "50% potential encounter hotspot") %>%
  hideGroup(map_groups)

fish_map <- fish_map %>%
  addLayersControl(overlayGroups = map_groups,
                   options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = TRUE)) %>%
  addLegend(position = "bottomright", colors = unname(fish_colors),
            labels = names(fish_colors), title = "Fish") %>%
  addControl("Solid: range estimate<br>Dashed: lower/upper 95% area CI limits",
             position = "bottomleft")

# Points show recorded locations. Toggle layers using the checkboxes.
# Enable the encounter hotspot to show where the fish are most likely to meet.
fish_map  # Displays in the RStudio Viewer.

# Save a shareable HTML map; the background tiles need an internet connection.
withr::with_dir("outputs/ctmm_example", {
  htmlwidgets::saveWidget(fish_map, "great_lake_map.html", selfcontained = TRUE)
})

```
